a: the elders with him
p: Polycarp writes with the elders of Smyrna and gives himself no title.
b: Greek presbyteroi, 'elders', the word behind 'presbyter' and 'priest'. Polycarp names himself and 'the elders with him' and calls himself nothing more. In chapters 5-6 he tells the Philippians to submit to 'the elders and deacons' and never mentions an overseer (episkopos, the word behind 'bishop'). Later writers call him the overseer of Smyrna: Eusebius says he was 'entrusted with the episcopate of the church of Smyrna' (Church History 3.36.1), and Irenaeus that apostles appointed him (Against Heresies 3.3.4). The Catholic Encyclopedia notes the contrast with Ignatius, who 'lays every stress upon episcopacy', while Polycarp's letter 'does not even mention it'. See the note at 5:3.
orig: οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ πρεσβύτεροι (hoi syn autō presbyteroi)

a: lives as a resident alien in
p: The Greek pictures the church as a foreigner living for a while in Philippi.
b: Greek paroikousē, from paroikos, a resident foreigner without citizen rights. The same opening stands at the head of 1 Clement 1:0 and the Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:0, and the word comes from the way 1 Peter speaks to Christians: 'live in fear during your time as resident aliens' (1 Peter 1:17); 'as resident aliens and temporary residents' (1 Peter 2:11). The church's true city is elsewhere. Polycarp makes the same point in 5:2 with the opposite picture: 'if we live as citizens worthy of him'. The word paroikia later became 'parish'.

a: Philippi
p: A Roman colony in Macedonia, where Paul founded a church (Acts 16:12-40).
b: Acts calls Philippi 'one of the foremost cities of its district of Macedonia, and a colony' (Acts 16:12). Paul founded the church there with Lydia's household and the jailer's family (Acts 16:13-40), and later wrote it the letter we call Philippians, thanking it for its 'partnership in the good news, from the first day right up to now' (Philippians 1:5). Polycarp writes some sixty or more years later. He knows the church's history: Paul taught there 'face to face' and wrote to it (3:2; 11:3), and its faith was 'spoken of since early times' (1:2).

a: may they be multiplied
t: The greeting of 1 Peter and Jude
p: Polycarp's blessing uses the closing word of the greetings in 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude.
b: Greek plēthyntheiē, 'may it be multiplied'. Paul's greetings say 'Grace to you and peace' and stop; the verb 'be multiplied' closes the greetings of 1 Peter 1:2 and 2 Peter 1:2 ("Grace to you, and peace: may they be multiplied") and Jude 2, which also has 'mercy': "Mercy to you, and peace, and love: may they be multiplied" (Jude 2). It is the first of many echoes of 1 Peter in the letter (see the note at 8:1). Eusebius noticed them: Polycarp 'has made use of certain testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter' (Church History 4.14.9).

a: the copies of true love
p: Greek mimēmata: 'imitations, copies'. Polycarp means the prisoners who passed through Philippi.
b: The noun mimēma is 'anything imitated, copy' (LSJ). Polycarp calls the chained prisoners 'the copies of true love': in their suffering they reproduce the love of Christ, who gave himself. English versions differ: Lightfoot has 'the followers of the true Love', taking 'Love' as Christ himself; Lake has 'followed the pattern of true love', applying the words to the Philippians. The Greek dexamenois ta mimēmata, 'having received the copies', makes the copies the people the Philippians welcomed. The Plain English Translation keeps 'copies' without adding a word, and a gloss says who they are.
orig: τὰ μιμήματα τῆς ἀληθοῦς ἀγάπης (ta mimēmata tēs alēthous agapēs)

a: chains fit for saints
t: Prisoners on the road to Rome
p: Ignatius of Antioch and others came through Philippi in chains on their way to die in Rome.
b: Polycarp names them in 9:1: 'the blessed Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus'. Eusebius tells that Ignatius, overseer of Antioch, was sent from Syria to Rome and 'became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ', and that he wrote letters from Smyrna, where Polycarp was, and then from Troas (Church History 3.36.3-10). In his letter to Polycarp Ignatius writes of his 'sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis' (Ignatius to Polycarp 8:1), the port of Philippi, the same route Paul took (Acts 16:11-12). The Philippians welcomed the prisoners and walked them on their way, as the custom of escorting travelers required (3 John 6).

a: those chains are the crowns
p: A prisoner's chains are royal headbands: the martyr wins the victor's crown.
b: Greek diadēmata, the cloth band a king wore, not the athlete's wreath (stephanos). Polycarp turns the shame of the prisoner into kingship: those who are 'truly chosen' wear their chains as royal crowns. The New Testament promises the faithful 'the crown of life' (Revelation 2:10, said to Polycarp's own church of Smyrna) and on Christ's head are 'many royal crowns' (Revelation 19:12). The Martyrdom of Polycarp later says Polycarp was 'crowned with the crown of incorruption' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:1).

a: untying the birth pains of Hades
p: Polycarp repeats Acts 2:24, but with 'Hades' where the Acts the site translates has 'death'.
b: Peter said at Pentecost: "God raised him, untying the birth pains of death" (Acts 2:24). Polycarp gives the same words, lysas tas ōdinas, 'untying the birth pains', but ends with tou hadou, 'of Hades', the place of the dead, where the SBLGNT and the Byzantine text of Acts both read tou thanatou, 'of death'. The Greek Psalm 17:6 (Psalm 18:5 in the site's numbering) has the same pair, ōdines hadou, 'birth pains of Hades', where the Hebrew has "The ropes of Sheol" (Psalm 18:5); Peter's sermon goes on to quote the Psalms (Acts 2:25-28). Polycarp may be blending Acts with that Psalm, or quoting from memory. The image is of death in labor, unable to hold the child it must give up.
orig: λύσας τὰς ὠδῖνας τοῦ ᾅδου (lysas tas ōdinas tou hadou)

a: He endured for our sins
p: The verb is hypomenō, 'endure', the word for the martyrs' staying power in 8:1-9:1.
b: Greek hypemeinen, 'he endured'. Polycarp ties Christ's death to the theme of the whole letter: Christ 'endured everything' (8:1), we are to imitate his 'endurance' (8:2), and the Philippians saw 'endurance' in Ignatius and the others (9:1). The Plain English Translation keeps 'endure' and 'endurance' for this word family, as the site's Romans and 4 Maccabees do.

a: a joy that words cannot tell, a joy made glorious
p: Polycarp borrows 1 Peter 1:8 almost word for word.
b: 1 Peter says: "You love him without having seen him. You do not see him even now, yet you believe in him and shout for joy, with a joy that words cannot tell, a joy made glorious" (1 Peter 1:8). Polycarp keeps 'joy that words cannot tell' (aneklalētō) and 'made glorious' (dedoxasmenē) and shortens the rest. The next words, 'Many long to enter into that joy', may echo 1 Peter 1:12, where 'angels would love to bend down and peer into' the good news.

a: it is by grace that you have been saved, not from works
t: Saved by grace, not from works
p: Polycarp quotes Ephesians 2 and agrees with it; in 2:2 he also says God will raise us 'if we do his will'.
b: Paul wrote: "It is by grace that you have been saved, through faith" and "It does not come from works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Polycarp's Greek, chariti este sesōsmenoi, ouk ex ergōn, is Paul's, with 'by the will of God through Jesus Christ' in place of 'through faith'. Compared with the Bible: this matches the 66 books. In the next verses he urges good works and says God will raise us 'if we do his will' (2:2), as Paul himself goes on to say we were made 'for good works' (Ephesians 2:10). The churches read that pairing differently; the site's cards at Ephesians 2, Romans 3 and James 2 set out the views.
orig: χάριτί ἐστε σεσωσμένοι, οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων (chariti este sesōsmenoi, ouk ex ergōn)

a: grace
p: Greek charis: the gift of kindness no one earned.
b: Greek chariti, 'by grace'. As across the site's New Testament, charis is 'grace', the undeserved favor of God. The word returns at the letter's close: 'Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ, in grace' (14:1).

a: tuck up your robes
p: A man tucked his long robe into his belt to work or run; 1 Peter 1:13 uses the same phrase.
b: Greek anazōsamenoi tas osphyas, 'having girded up your loins'. 1 Peter 1:13 says "So tuck up the robes of your mind and get ready to move" (1 Peter 1:13); Polycarp drops 'of your mind' and keeps the plain picture. The rest of the verse leans on 1 Peter too: 'the one who raised ... from the dead and gave him glory' is 1 Peter 1:21 ("who raised him from among the dead and gave him glory").
orig: ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας ὑμῶν (anazōsamenoi tas osphyas hymōn)

a: serve God in fear and in truth
p: 'Serve the LORD in fear' (Psalm 2:11), with 'in truth' added.
b: The Greek Psalm 2:11 reads douleusate tō kyriō en phobō, the Hebrew "Serve the LORD in fear" (Psalm 2:11). Polycarp has 'serve God' and adds 'and in truth', much as Joshua's farewell pairs serving God with integrity and faithfulness (Joshua 24:14). The verb douleuō is the service of a slave; the letter returns to it in 6:3: 'let us serve him with fear and all reverence'.

a: All things in heaven and on earth were put under him
p: Paul's language for Christ's rule: Philippians 2:10, Philippians 3:21 and 1 Corinthians 15:27.
b: Lake's margin points to Philippians 3:21 (the power 'to put all things under himself') and Philippians 2:10 (every knee 'of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth'). The verb hypetagē, 'were subjected', is the one in 1 Corinthians 15:27: "All things have been put under him" (1 Corinthians 15:27), from Psalm 8:6. Polycarp is writing to the church that received Philippians, and he uses its own words.
orig: ὑπετάγη τὰ πάντα ἐπουράνια καὶ ἐπίγεια (hypetagē ta panta epourania kai epigeia)

a: every breathing thing worships him
p: The last line of the Psalms, now said of Christ.
b: The Psalter ends: "Let every breathing thing praise Yah!" (Psalm 150:6). Polycarp gives the same scope, pasa pnoē, 'every breath', and the verb latreuei, 'serves in worship', and the one worshiped is the risen Christ. He speaks of Christ in the words used of God.
orig: ᾧ πᾶσα πνοὴ λατρεύει (hō pasa pnoē latreuei)

a: judge of the living and the dead
p: A phrase from the early preaching: Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5.
b: Peter tells Cornelius that God 'has marked him out to judge the living and the dead' (Acts 10:42); the phrase returns in 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5 and later in the creeds ('he will come again to judge the living and the dead'). Polycarp sets the warning beside it: God 'will demand his blood from those who refuse to obey him'. The letter keeps the judgment in view (6:2; 7:1; 11:2).

a: God will demand his blood from those who refuse to obey him
p: Polycarp lays the guilt on all who disobey, not on one people.
b: The phrase 'demand blood from' (ekzēteō) is the language of Genesis 9:5 and of Jesus' warning that 'this generation is called to account for the blood of every prophet' (Luke 11:50). Polycarp does not name any people here: those who answer for Christ's blood are 'those who refuse to obey him', whoever they are. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, by contrast, singles out 'the Jews' among his enemies (Martyrdom of Polycarp 13:1). Compare Hebrews 10:29.

a: The one who raised him from the dead will raise us too
p: 2 Corinthians 4:14 and 1 Corinthians 6:14: Christ's resurrection is the pledge of ours.
b: Paul wrote that 'the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus' (2 Corinthians 4:14) and that "God both raised the Lord and will raise us up through his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Polycarp adds a condition: 'if we do his will, walk in his commands, and love what he loved'. He means that the resurrection to life is for those who live as Christ's people (compare John 5:29); he does not say how the condition relates to grace (see the note at 1:3). Those who deny the resurrection are the 'firstborn of Satan' (7:1).

a: love of money
t: Love of money: the letter's theme
p: Greek philargyria. Five warnings in the Greek, two in the Latin; it is what brought down Valens (11:1-2).
b: The word philargyria, 'love of silver', appears in 2:2, 4:1, 4:3 and 6:1; deacons must be 'not money-loving' (5:2); and the Latin of 11:1-2 warns twice against avaritia, 'greed', in the case of the elder Valens. The Plain English Translation renders philargyria 'love of money', as the site's 1 Timothy 6:10 does. Read from the end, the warnings of chapters 2-6 prepare for chapter 11.

a: or abuse for abuse, or punch for punch
p: 1 Peter 3:9 with one item added: 'punch for punch'.
b: "Do not give back evil for evil or abuse for abuse" (1 Peter 3:9); compare Romans 12:17. Polycarp adds gronthon anti gronthou, 'fist for fist', a blunt picture of a brawl, and 'curse for curse', which recalls Jesus' 'Bless the ones who curse you' (Luke 6:28). The list leads straight into the Lord's own words in 2:3.

a: Do not judge, so that you are not judged
t: The Lord's words, in a form of their own
p: Polycarp's saying stands between Matthew 7, Luke 6 and 1 Clement 13:2.
b: The first line is the Greek of Matthew 7:1 exactly: Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte. The rest is in no Gospel in this form: aphiete, kai aphethēsetai hymin ('Forgive, and you will be forgiven'), where Luke 6:37 has 'Release, and you will be released'; eleate, hina eleēthēte ('Show mercy, so that you will be shown mercy'), where Luke 6:36 has 'Become compassionate'. 1 Clement 13:2 has the same two lines, Eleate, hina eleēthēte; aphiete, hina aphethē hymin, in another order, also as words 'the Lord' spoke. The measure saying is Luke 6:38's antimetrēthēsetai. Whether both letters drew on oral teaching, a written collection, or the Gospels quoted from memory cannot be settled from these texts.

a: remember what the Lord said when he taught
p: He introduces the Lord's words as remembered teaching, not as 'it is written'.
b: Greek mnēmoneuontes de hōn eipen ho kyrios didaskōn, 'remembering what the Lord said, teaching'. Paul uses a like formula in Acts 20:35: 'we must keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus'. Polycarp quotes Jesus again in 7:2 ('just as the Lord said'). He calls none of these sayings Scripture; the one passage he introduces as 'these Scriptures' is 12:1. Irenaeus later said Polycarp told what he had heard from John 'and from the others who had seen the Lord' (Eusebius, Church History 5.20.6).
orig: μνημονεύοντες δὲ ὧν εἶπεν ὁ κύριος διδάσκων

a: Blessed are the poor, and those who are persecuted on account of righteousness
p: Luke's 'Blessed are the poor' joined to Matthew's blessing on the persecuted.
b: Luke has "Blessed are the poor, because the kingdom of God is yours" (Luke 6:20); Matthew has 'Blessed are those who are poor in spirit' and 'Blessed are those who have suffered persecution on account of righteousness, because the kingdom of heaven is theirs' (Matthew 5:3, 10). Polycarp joins the first and last beatitudes. His 'poor' has no 'in spirit', like Luke; his 'persecuted on account of righteousness' and 'is theirs' are like Matthew; his 'kingdom of God' is Luke's word, not Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven'.

a: you asked me first
p: The Philippians had written to Polycarp; his letter answers theirs.
b: Greek proepekalesasthe, 'you called on me beforehand'. The Philippians' letter is lost, but Polycarp's reply shows what they asked: to be taught 'about righteousness' (3:1), to have their letter carried to Syria (13:1), and to receive copies of Ignatius's letters (13:2). Lake's footnote at 12:1 thinks the words 'you are well trained in the sacred writings' are quoted from their letter. The Catholic Encyclopedia sums up the three requests the same way.

a: he wrote you letters
t: One letter to the Philippians, or more?
p: Polycarp says Paul wrote the Philippians 'letters', plural; in 11:3 the Latin has 'his letter'.
b: The New Testament has one letter of Paul to the Philippians. Polycarp's Greek here is plural, epistolas, but the Latin of 11:3 says the Philippians are 'at the beginning of his letter' (singular), and Lake's footnote there guesses the lost Greek had a plural. Readers have suggested: Polycarp knew more than one letter of Paul to Philippi, now lost or joined into our Philippians; he counted letters to the Macedonian churches together (11:3 echoes 2 Thessalonians 1:4); or he used the plural loosely for one letter. The text shows only that he believed Paul's writing to Philippi was there for them to study.

a: the wisdom of blessed and glorious Paul
p: Polycarp names Paul four times, and his letter draws on many of Paul's letters.
b: Paul is 'blessed and glorious' here, 'Paul himself' among the martyrs (9:1), 'the blessed Paul' who worked among the Philippians (11:3), and the teacher of 1 Corinthians 6:2 (11:2). Polycarp humbly puts himself below Paul: no one 'like me' can keep up with him. The Catholic Encyclopedia quotes Lightfoot: in Polycarp's letter 'sentence after sentence is frequently made up of passages from the Evangelical and Apostolic writings', and its quotations are 'incomparably more numerous' than in the much longer letters of Ignatius. George Reid's article on the canon in the same encyclopedia counts 'eight of St. Paul's writings' cited by Polycarp.

a: That faith is the mother of us all
p: Paul said the Jerusalem above is 'our mother'; Polycarp says it of faith, in the words of the Byzantine text.
b: Galatians 4:26 says of the Jerusalem above: "She is our mother" (Galatians 4:26) in the critical text the site follows, while the Byzantine text and the KJV read 'the mother of us all' (the site's variant entry there). Polycarp's hētis estin mētēr pantōn hēmōn is word for word the longer reading, and he applies it to faith. So his letter is an early witness to the wording the Byzantine manuscripts have, or to a familiar phrase that a scribe of Galatians could also have taken up.
orig: ἥτις ἐστὶν μήτηρ πάντων ἡμῶν (hētis estin mētēr pantōn hēmōn)

a: with hope following behind it and love going ahead of it
p: Paul's three, set in a procession.
b: Paul ends 1 Corinthians 13: "But now these three last: faith, hope and love. The greatest of them is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13). Polycarp pictures the three walking together: faith in the middle, hope behind, love in front. Love leads because, as he says next, love fulfills the command: compare Romans 13:8, "Whoever loves the other person has fulfilled the law" (Romans 13:8), and Galatians 5:14.

a: Love of money is where every trouble begins
p: Polycarp gives 1 Timothy 6:10 and 6:7 with small changes.
b: The site's 1 Timothy 6:10 reads "A root of every kind of evil is the love of money" (1 Timothy 6:10). Polycarp has archē, 'beginning', for 'root', and chalepōn, 'hard things, troubles', for 'evils'. The next line is 1 Timothy 6:7, "We carried nothing into the world, because we cannot carry anything out of it either" (1 Timothy 6:7), introduced with 'we know that', as a saying the readers share. Lake's margin also lists Job 1:21. Polycarp draws on 1 and 2 Timothy again in 5:2, 9:2, 11:4 and 12:3.
orig: Ἀρχὴ δὲ πάντων χαλεπῶν φιλαργυρία (Archē de pantōn chalepōn philargyria)

a: the weapons of righteousness
p: Paul's phrase from 2 Corinthians 6:7 and Romans 6:13.
b: Paul served 'with the weapons of righteousness, right-handed and left-handed' (2 Corinthians 6:7), and told the Romans to hand over their bodies to God 'as weapons of righteousness' (Romans 6:13). Polycarp's hoplois tēs dikaiosynēs is the same phrase. He makes it a call to the leaders first: 'let us first teach ourselves'.

a: Then let us teach our wives
p: Wives, widows, deacons, young men, virgins, elders: Polycarp's list of duties, like the New Testament household codes.
b: Chapters 4-6 move from group to group, as Ephesians 5:22-6:9, Colossians 3:18-4:1, 1 Timothy 3 and 5, Titus 2 and 1 Peter 2-3 do. Two things stand out. Polycarp speaks to the men about teaching their wives, not to the wives; and his list is mostly about church groups (widows, deacons, virgins, elders) rather than the household (no slaves or masters). The virtues are the common ones of those codes: faithfulness in marriage, self-control, raising children in the fear of God (compare Ephesians 6:4).

a: they are God's altar
p: The widows' prayers and the gifts given to them rise to God like offerings on an altar.
b: Greek thysiastērion theou. Widows supported by the church were to pray 'for everyone without stopping' (compare 1 Timothy 5:5: 'She stays with her pleas and prayers night and day'). Polycarp calls them God's altar: what the church gives them, and the prayers they offer, are like sacrifices laid there, and every sacrifice must be without blemish, so the widows must keep themselves from slander and greed. Polycarp uses the image without explaining it.

a: Everything is checked for blemishes
p: Greek mōmoskopeitai: the word for examining an animal for flaws before it is offered.
b: The verb mōmoskopeō comes from mōmos, 'blemish', and skopeō, 'look at'. Pape's lexicon defines it as examining, especially sacrificial animals, to see whether they are without fault, and LSJ defines the noun mōmoskopos as 'looking for blemishes in sacrificial victims'. The law required an offering to be 'flawless to be accepted' (Leviticus 22:21). Polycarp keeps the altar picture going: God inspects every offering, and nothing hidden escapes him. Lake's English 'all offerings are tested' makes the picture explicit.

a: not one of the secrets of the heart
p: The phrase of 1 Corinthians 14:25: God sees what is hidden.
b: Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 14:25, where a visitor finds 'the secrets of his heart come into the open'. Polycarp's ta krypta tēs kardias is the same phrase. Compare Romans 2:16, the day 'when God judges what people keep secret', and Hebrews 4:13.

a: God is not sneered at
p: Polycarp quotes Galatians 6:7 with 'We know that'.
b: "Do not be led astray. God is not sneered at. Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). The Greek theos ou myktērizetai is the same as Galatians; myktērizō is literally 'turn up the nose at'. As in 4:1 and 6:1, Polycarp introduces a familiar line with 'knowing that' (eidotes hoti).

a: deacons
t: Deacons and the servant of all
p: Greek diakonos is both 'deacon' and 'servant', and Polycarp plays on the two.
b: Polycarp tells the diakonoi, the deacons, to live by the truth of the Lord, 'who became the diakonos of all'. The site renders the church office 'deacon' (as in Philippians 1:1, 'with overseers and deacons') and other uses 'servant', so the play has to be noted: the deacons' model is Christ the servant (Mark 9:35: 'everyone's servant'; Mark 10:45). Many of the qualities match 1 Timothy 3:8-13 word for word in the Greek: 'not double-worded' (dilogoi), which the site's 1 Timothy 3:8 renders 'They should not say one thing to one person and another to the next'.

a: if we live as citizens worthy of him
p: The verb Paul used to the same church: 'live as citizens worthy of the good news' (Philippians 1:27).
b: Greek politeusōmetha, from politēs, 'citizen'. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud of it (Acts 16:12, 21). Paul wrote to them: "live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ" (Philippians 1:27), and "we belong to a commonwealth in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). Polycarp uses the same verb in a letter to the same city. The promise that follows, "we will also reign with him", is 2 Timothy 2:12.
orig: ἐὰν πολιτευσώμεθα ἀξίως αὐτοῦ (ean politeusōmetha axiōs autou)

a: Please him in this present age, and we will also receive the age to come
p: Greek aiōn, 'age': the present age and the one to come.
b: Greek en tō nyn aiōni ... kai ton mellonta, 'in the now age ... also the coming one'. The New Testament contrasts 'this age' and 'the age to come' (Matthew 12:32; Ephesians 1:21). Polycarp promises the coming age to those who please Christ now, and in 9:2 praises the martyrs who did not love 'the present age'.
orig: ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι (en tō nyn aiōni)

a: every desire wages war against the Spirit
t: War against the Spirit, or the spirit?
p: 1 Peter says desires war 'against the soul'; Polycarp says 'against the spirit', as in Galatians 5:17.
b: Greek kata tou pneumatos. 1 Peter 2:11 warns against 'the flesh's desires. They are at war with the soul', using the same verb strateuomai, 'wage war'. Paul in Galatians 5:17 writes that the flesh desires 'what is against the Spirit'. Polycarp's pneuma could mean God's Spirit (as Galatians) or the human spirit (as the 'spirit' of 7:2, 'The spirit is eager'). The Plain English Translation capitalizes it as in Galatians, the closer wording; the other reading is possible.
orig: κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος στρατεύεται (kata tou pneumatos strateuetai)

a: neither those who commit sexual sin, nor soft men, nor men who lie with males will inherit the kingdom of God
p: Three items from Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, in the site's wording.
b: Polycarp's Greek oute pornoi oute malakoi oute arsenokoitai basileian theou klēronomēsousin takes three words from 1 Corinthians 6:9 and the closing verb from 6:10. The Plain English Translation uses the site's renderings of the three words in 1 Corinthians 6:9, where the note explains malakoi, 'soft men', and arsenokoitai, 'men who lie with males', and the debate over what they cover. Polycarp addresses the 'younger men' and adds his own last item: 'nor will those who do what is out of place' (ta atopa).
orig: οὔτε πόρνοι οὔτε μαλακοὶ οὔτε ἀρσενοκοῖται

a: submit to the elders and deacons as to God and Christ
t: Elders and deacons, but no overseer
p: Philippi's leaders, in Polycarp's telling, are elders and deacons; he never names an overseer there.
b: Ignatius, writing to Smyrna in the same years, says: 'See that you all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as you would the apostles' (To the Smyrnaeans 8, ANF translation). Polycarp's phrase is like it, 'as to God and Christ', but names only elders and deacons. The letter itself does not explain this. Possible readings: Philippi was still led by a council of elders, as Paul's 'overseers and deacons' (Philippians 1:1) could suggest; or its overseer had died or was not in view; or Polycarp counted himself one of the elders (1:0) and used the older names. The churches' views on bishops and elders are on the cards at Philippians 1, 1 Timothy 3 and Acts 20.

a: The virgins
p: Unmarried young women, here treated as a group in the church.
b: Greek tas parthenous. Paul speaks of 'the unmarried woman, the virgin' who is concerned 'with the things of the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:34). Polycarp gives the virgins one line, a 'blameless and pure conscience'. Whether they were simply the church's unmarried girls or a recognized group of women vowed to stay unmarried, the letter does not say. Ignatius greets at Smyrna 'the virgins who are called widows' (To the Smyrnaeans 13, ANF), which shows the two groups could overlap.

a: They must turn back those who have wandered off and visit all who are sick
p: The elders are to do what Ezekiel's bad shepherds failed to do.
b: Ezekiel accused Israel's shepherds: 'You have not healed the sick ... You have not brought back the strays' (Ezekiel 34:4), and God promised, "The stray one I will bring home" (Ezekiel 34:16). Polycarp gives the elders that task: epistrephontes ta apopeplanēmena, 'turning back the things gone astray', and visiting the sick. The care of 'a widow or an orphan or a poor man' is James 1:27's 'to visit orphans and widows'. Pope Leo XIV quotes the opening of 6:1 in his exhortation Dilexi te (2025), paragraph 39, with a line of Ignatius, and concludes: 'From these two witnesses, we see that the Church appears as a mother of the poor'.

a: plan ahead for what is good before God and people
p: The Greek of Proverbs 3:4, which Paul also used.
b: Greek pronoountes aei tou kalou enōpion theou kai anthrōpōn. Lake's margin gives Proverbs 3:4, with 2 Corinthians 8:21 and Romans 12:17. The site's Proverbs 3:4, from the Hebrew, reads 'favor and good insight in the eyes of God and of people'; the Greek Proverbs speaks of planning good things, and Paul uses that form: "We plan ahead for what is good, not only before the Lord but also before people" (2 Corinthians 8:21). Polycarp's words are closest to Paul's.

a: we all owe a debt of sin
p: Lake: 'knowing that' marks a quotation, but its source is unknown.
b: Greek pantes opheiletai esmen hamartias, 'all debtors we are of sin'. Lake's footnote: 'The introductory formula "knowing that" renders it probable that these words are a quotation, but the source is unknown.' The idea of sin as a debt is the Lord's Prayer's: "And forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven the people who owe us" (Matthew 6:12). That is why Polycarp goes straight on to forgiveness (6:2).
orig: πάντες ὀφειλέται ἐσμὲν ἁμαρτίας (pantes opheiletai esmen hamartias)

a: every one of us must stand at Christ's judgment seat
p: Polycarp joins two of Paul's sayings and says 'of Christ'.
b: Romans 14:10 says 'We will all stand in front of God's judgment seat' (where the Byzantine text has 'of Christ'), and Romans 14:12, 'each of us will give an account to God about ourselves'. 2 Corinthians 5:10 says 'all of us must be shown openly before the judgment seat of Christ'. Polycarp's sentence uses Romans' verb 'stand before' (parastēnai) and 2 Corinthians' 'judgment seat of Christ'. A bēma was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave judgment.
orig: τῷ βήματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ (tō bēmati tou Christou)

a: the eyes of the Lord and God
p: 'The Lord and God' may be Christ called both, or the Lord Christ and God the Father.
b: Greek tōn tou kyriou kai theou esmen ophthalmōn, with one article for both nouns. It may mean one person, 'the Lord and God' (Christ, as in 12:2, 'our Lord and God Jesus Christ', and John 20:28, "My Lord and my God!"), or two, 'the Lord' (Christ) and 'God' (the Father). In the next words the judgment seat is 'of Christ', which suits either reading. The Plain English Translation keeps the ambiguity.
orig: τῶν τοῦ κυρίου καὶ θεοῦ ἐσμὲν ὀφθαλμῶν

a: the apostles who brought us the good news, and the prophets
p: Most likely the Old Testament prophets, who 'announced ahead of time' the Lord's coming.
b: Polycarp names three authorities: the Lord's own command, the apostles who preached to 'us' (euangelisamenoi, 'brought good news', the word behind 'gospel'), and the prophets who 'announced ahead of time the coming of our Lord'. That last phrase fits the Hebrew prophets, as in 2 Peter 3:2: 'the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets, and the command your apostles passed on from the Lord'. Christian prophets (Ephesians 2:20; 4:11) are the other possible reading. Irenaeus held that Polycarp himself had been 'instructed by apostles' (Against Heresies 3.3.4).

a: false brothers
p: Paul's word for intruders in the church (Galatians 2:4).
b: Greek pseudadelphōn, the word of Galatians 2:4 ('the false brothers who were slipped in') and 2 Corinthians 11:26. Polycarp joins them with those who 'carry the name of the Lord as hypocrites' and 'lead empty-headed people astray'. He names no one; chapter 7 says what they teach.

a: everyone who does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is an antichrist
p: Polycarp's sentence joins 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7.
b: 1 John says: 'any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God, and any spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is what belongs to the antichrist' (1 John 4:2-3); 2 John 7 says of the deniers, 'This one is the deceiver and the antichrist'. Polycarp's en sarki elēlythenai, 'to have come in the flesh', has the perfect tense of 1 John 4:2. He turns John's test of spirits into a rule for persons, without the article: 'is an antichrist'. The teachers in view denied that Christ had a real body. Ignatius, in Smyrna, attacked those who said 'He only seemed to suffer' (To the Smyrnaeans 2, ANF).
orig: ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθέναι, ἀντιχριστός ἐστιν (en sarki elēlythenai, antichristos estin)

a: the testimony of the cross
p: Greek to martyrion tou staurou: the witness the cross gives that Christ truly suffered and died.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps 'testimony' for martyrion here (in the Martyrdom of Polycarp the same word family means 'martyrdom'). Two senses are possible: the witness the cross bears, that Christ really died in the flesh (against those who said his suffering only seemed real); or the witness Christ himself gave on the cross (compare 1 Timothy 6:13, Christ's 'good confession' before Pilate). Either way, the cross is evidence that must be confessed, and refusing it is to be 'from the devil' (compare 1 John 3:8).
orig: τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ σταυροῦ (to martyrion tou staurou)

a: bends the Lord's sayings to fit his own desires
p: Greek methodeuō: to work something by craft, to 'get round' it.
b: The verb methodeuō (from methodos, 'method') means to 'treat by rule or method' and also to 'employ craft' or to 'get round' someone (LSJ). Polycarp means teachers who handle the logia, 'sayings', of the Lord cleverly to serve their own desires. 2 Peter 3:16 says the same of people who twist Paul's letters 'as they do the other Scriptures'.
orig: μεθοδεύῃ τὰ λόγια τοῦ κυρίου (methodeuē ta logia tou kyriou)

a: says there is no resurrection and no judgment
p: The same denial Paul met at Corinth and in 2 Timothy.
b: Paul asked the Corinthians: 'how is it that some among you say no resurrection of the dead exists?' (1 Corinthians 15:12). 2 Timothy 2:18 names men 'claiming that the resurrection has already taken place'. Polycarp pairs resurrection and judgment, as in 2:1-2: if there is no rising, there is no judgment to fear, and life may be lived 'to fit his own desires'.

a: that person is the firstborn of Satan
t: The firstborn of Satan, and Marcion
p: Irenaeus says Polycarp once called Marcion 'the first-born of Satan' to his face.
b: Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, tells that 'Polycarp himself replied to Marcion, who met him on one occasion, and said, Do you know me? I do know you, the first-born of Satan' (Against Heresies 3.3.4, ANF translation; Eusebius quotes it, Church History 4.14.7). Lake's footnote: the phrase 'was applied, presumably later, by Polycarp to Marcion'. Did the letter already mean Marcion? P. N. Harrison argued so (1936) and held to it in his reply of 1948, where he names C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd as accepting his two letters but denying 'any reference to Marcion', and Carl Schneider (1937) as having 'no doubt about the reference to Marcion'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Harnack, who once seemed to bring the date down for this reason, came to admit that 'there need be no reference to Marcion at all', and gives Lightfoot's reasons: 'nothing is said about his characteristic errors, e.g., the distinction between the God of the Old and the God of the New Testament', and 'the antinomianism ascribed to "the first-born of Satan" is inapplicable to the austere Marcion'. See the chapter page.
orig: πρωτότοκός ἐστι τοῦ σατανᾶ (prōtotokos esti tou satana)

a: the word that was passed on to us at the start
p: Polycarp's answer to false teaching: go back to what was handed down at first.
b: Greek ton ex archēs hēmin paradothenta logon, 'the word handed down to us from the beginning'. 1 John answers its false teachers the same way: 'what you heard from the beginning must remain in you' (1 John 2:24); Jude urges a fight for the faith 'handed down to the saints once for all' (Jude 3). The verb paradidōmi is the root of 'tradition'. Irenaeus later appealed to Polycarp as a man who 'always taught the things which he had learned from the apostles' (Against Heresies 3.3.4).
orig: τὸν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡμῖν παραδοθέντα λόγον

a: Let us keep a clear head for prayer
p: Another phrase of 1 Peter.
b: Greek nēphontes pros tas euchas; 1 Peter 4:7 has nēpsate eis proseuchas: "So be sensible and keep a clear head for prayer" (1 Peter 4:7). Polycarp adds fasting, as Jesus assumed his disciples would fast (Matthew 6:16-18).

a: not to bring us into testing
p: Polycarp quotes the Lord's Prayer and then Jesus' words in Gethsemane.
b: "And do not bring us into testing" (Matthew 6:13) is the Greek mē eisenenkēs hēmas eis peirasmon; Polycarp has the same verb and noun in a request to 'the all-seeing God'. Then, 'just as the Lord said': To men pneuma prothymon, hē de sarx asthenēs, the Greek of Matthew 26:41 and Mark 14:38 exactly, which the site renders "The spirit is eager, the flesh weak" (Matthew 26:41). In the Gospels Jesus says it to the sleeping disciples in Gethsemane; Polycarp makes it the reason to pray. The Martyrdom later shows him praying for hours before his arrest (Martyrdom of Polycarp 7:2-3).

a: the down payment of our righteousness
p: Greek arrabōn: the first installment that guarantees the rest.
b: Paul calls the Spirit a arrabōn: 'This Spirit is a down payment on our inheritance' (Ephesians 1:14; compare 2 Corinthians 1:22). Polycarp gives the word to Christ himself: he is the down payment of 'our righteousness', the first part of a righteousness we will have in full. The Plain English Translation uses 'down payment' as in Paul. 'Christ Jesus our hope' is 1 Timothy 1:1.
orig: τῷ ἀρραβῶνι τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἡμῶν (tō arrabōni tēs dikaiosynēs hēmōn)

a: carried our sins up in his own body onto the tree
p: Polycarp quotes 1 Peter 2:24 and 2:22, which themselves draw on Isaiah 53.
b: "He himself carried our sins up in his body onto the tree" (1 Peter 2:24). Polycarp's Greek has tō idiō sōmati, 'in his own body', where 1 Peter has en tō sōmati autou, 'in his body'; the Plain English Translation keeps the site's wording with 'own'. The next line is 1 Peter 2:22 exactly: "He did no sin, nor was trickery found in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22), from Isaiah 53:9 ('no deceit was in his mouth'). 'Carried our sins' recalls Isaiah 53:12: "He bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). Eusebius had passages like these in mind when he wrote that Polycarp used 'testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter' (Church History 4.14.9).

a: the model to trace
p: Greek hypogrammos: the line of letters a child traces when learning to write.
b: LSJ gives 'writing-copy, pattern, model', and cites 1 Peter 2:21, where the site renders the same word 'He left behind for you a model to trace, so that you would follow in his tracks'. Polycarp uses it just after quoting 1 Peter 2:22-24 (8:1), so the picture is Peter's. The 'imitation' of Christ's endurance (mimētai) leads into the examples of chapter 9, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp makes the same point about Polycarp himself (Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:2).

a: if we suffer for his name, let us give him glory
p: 1 Peter 4:16: suffering as a Christian is a reason to glorify God.
b: "But if it is for being a Christian, there is no shame in it. Let him give glory to God in this matter" (1 Peter 4:16). Compare Acts 5:41, where the apostles left the council glad 'because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name'. Polycarp's own trial, as the Martyrdom tells it, turns on that name: 'I am a Christian' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 10:1).

a: the blessed Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus
p: Ignatius, overseer of Antioch, and two companions, taken to Rome to die.
b: Eusebius quotes these verses to show that Polycarp knew Ignatius (Church History 3.36.13). Ignatius, he says, was 'chosen bishop of Antioch, second in succession to Peter', sent from Syria to Rome, 'food for wild beasts' (3.36.2-3). Of Zosimus and Rufus nothing more is told in the texts opened for this page. Rufus was a common name; nothing ties this Rufus to the son of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21) or the Rufus Paul greets (Romans 16:13). Polycarp calls them 'blessed' (makarios) and ranks these three with 'Paul himself and the other apostles'.

a: in Paul himself
p: The Philippians had seen Paul beaten and jailed in their own city.
b: Acts tells that at Philippi Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and put in the stocks (Acts 16:22-24), and Paul reminded the Philippians: "You are in the same contest you once watched me fight" (Philippians 1:30). Polycarp counts Paul's endurance as something the Philippians 'saw right in front of' them, in the city's own memory. By his time Paul and 'the other apostles' had died, and tradition remembered Paul as a martyr in Rome (compare 1 Clement 5:5-7).

a: ran for nothing
p: Polycarp uses Philippians 2:16, Paul's hope that he 'did not run for nothing'.
b: Paul wrote to this church that their faith would be 'proof that I did not run for nothing and did not work hard for nothing' (Philippians 2:16). Polycarp says the martyrs, Paul among them, did not run 'for nothing' (eis kenon), and 'the present age' that they did not love is from 2 Timothy 4:10, where Demas 'loved the present age'. The 'place owed to them' (ton opheilomenon autois topon) is the phrase 1 Clement 5:4 uses of Peter, who went 'to the place of glory owed' him.

a: they are in the place owed to them
p: Here Ignatius is with the Lord; in 13:2 Polycarp asks for news of him. One letter, or two?
b: In 9:1-2 Ignatius is among those who 'are in the place owed to them, with the Lord, with whom they also suffered'. In 13:2 Polycarp asks for anything certain about 'Ignatius himself and those who are with him'. The Catholic Encyclopedia takes the whole letter as written before Polycarp had heard of Ignatius' death, so that 9:2 counts on what was sure to come. P. N. Harrison (1936) argued instead that chapter 13 is an early 'Covering Note' and chapters 1-12 a later 'Crisis Letter'. In his 1948 reply he names C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd as agreeing 'that Polycarp wrote two letters, one before, the other after, the death of Ignatius', though they put the second only months or a year or two after the first. Lake (1912) treats the letter as one 'covering letter'. See the chapter page for chapter 13.

a: and was raised by God for our sake
p: The eight Greek manuscripts break off in this sentence; the rest comes from Eusebius and the Latin.
b: Lake's footnote at 9:2: 'Here G breaks off, but the rest of the sentence is given by L Eus.' G is the shared ancestor of the eight Greek manuscripts, L the old Latin version, and Eus. Eusebius, who quotes 9:1-2 in full (Church History 3.36.13). From 10:1 to 12:3 only the Latin survives, and the Plain English Translation there translates the Latin (see the note at 10:1). Eusebius quotes again from 13:1.

a: Stand in these things, then
t: From here, a translation of a translation
p: Polycarp's Greek is lost for 10:1-12:3, the end of 13:2 and 14:1. The Plain English Translation follows the old Latin.
b: Lake: the letter survives in eight Greek manuscripts, all defective, in 'two long quotations in Eusebius', and in a Latin version within the Latin collection of Ignatius's letters (his introduction). For chapters 10-12, the last sentence of 13:2 and chapter 14, only the Latin has the text, so the Plain English Translation here is made from a Latin translation of Polycarp's Greek, not from his own words. Where the Latin gives a phrase that also stands in the Greek New Testament, as 1 Peter 2:12 and Ephesians 4:26 do, the notes compare the two (see the notes at 10:2 and 12:1), but the Greek Polycarp wrote can only be guessed.

a: Wait on one another with the gentleness of the Lord
p: Latin praestolantes: 'waiting for, attending on'; Lake and Lightfoot say 'forestalling one another'.
b: The Latin mansuetudine domini alterutri praestolantes is hard. Praestolor means to wait for or to stand ready for someone. Lake and Lightfoot both render 'forestalling one another in the gentleness of the Lord', as if the Latin translated a Greek word like 'going before one another' (compare Romans 12:10: 'Each of you be first to honor the other'). The Plain English Translation keeps the Latin's ordinary sense, 'wait on', ready to serve. The lost Greek may have said something else.

a: Be firm in the faith and unchanging
p: Echoes of Colossians 1:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:58.
b: Lake's margin: Colossians 1:23 ('if you stay in the faith, with your foundation laid and standing firm') and 1 Corinthians 15:58 ('be steady, unmovable'). The phrases that follow, 'lovers of the family of believers, loving one another', echo 1 Peter 3:8 ('love like brothers'), 1 Peter 2:17 ('Love the brothers') and Jesus' command in John 13:34. The Latin fraternitatis amatores is literally 'lovers of the brotherhood'.

a: alms rescue from death
p: Polycarp quotes Tobit, a book of the Catholic Bible that the Anglican and Reformed confessions do not count as Scripture.
b: Latin eleemosyna de morte liberat, 'almsgiving frees from death'. Lake's margin gives Tobit 4:10 and 12:9, where the site's Tobit reads 'For alms rescue from death' (Tobit 4:10). Polycarp gives no formula ('it is written'); he states it as a known truth. Compared with the Bible: the 66 books praise giving to the poor (Proverbs 19:17; Luke 12:33) and Daniel tells a king to break with his sins 'by doing what is right' (Daniel 4:27), but none says alms rescue from death. Tobit ('Tobias') is in the Council of Trent's list of the Old Testament. Article VI of the Church of England reads it among the books the Church reads 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but does not 'apply them to establish any doctrine'; the Westminster Confession counts the books 'commonly called Apocrypha' as 'no part of the canon of Scripture'. Whether good works atone for sin is the question of the site's cards at Proverbs 16 and Tobit 4.
r: Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9; Proverbs 16:6; Proverbs 19:17; Daniel 4:27; 1 Peter 4:8

a: Keep your way of life beyond blame among the Gentiles
p: The Latin follows 1 Peter 2:12 closely.
b: "Keep your way of life fine and good among the Gentiles" (1 Peter 2:12), so that outsiders see 'your good works'. The Latin conversationem vestram irreprensibilem habentes in gentibus, ut ex bonis operibus vestris has the same order: way of life, among the Gentiles, good works. 'Submit to one another' before it is 1 Peter 5:5 and Ephesians 5:21. 'The Gentiles' here are the non-Christian people of the city.

a: the Lord is not insulted because of you
p: Lake's margin: Isaiah 52:5. Romans 2:24 gives the same verse in its Greek form.
b: The site's Isaiah 52:5, from the Hebrew, ends 'my name is treated with contempt'. The Greek Isaiah adds 'because of you ... among the Gentiles', and Paul quotes that form: "The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you" (Romans 2:24). Polycarp's 'the Lord is not insulted because of you' (Latin dominus in vobis non blasphemetur) and the woe of 10:3 take up the same idea: a church's behavior can bring its Lord's name into contempt.

a: woe to the one through whom the name of the Lord is insulted
p: The form of Jesus' woe in Matthew 18:7, applied to the Lord's name.
b: Jesus said: "woe to the person through whom the snare comes!" (Matthew 18:7). Polycarp's Latin, Vae autem, per quem nomen domini blasphematur, uses the same frame: woe to the one 'through whom' harm comes. No book of the Bible has this exact saying; it may be Polycarp's own line, built on Isaiah 52:5 (10:2).

a: to live with a clear head
p: Latin sobrietas, 'soberness', the clear head of 7:2 and 11:4.
b: Latin sobrietatem ergo docete omnes, in qua et vos conversamini, 'teach all soberness, in which you also live'. The Plain English Translation keeps the 'clear head' of 7:2 ('keep a clear head for prayer', Greek nēphontes) and 11:4 ('keep a level head', Latin sobrii) and does not use 'self-control', which it keeps for Greek enkrateia (4:2; 5:2). Lightfoot's English has 'teach all men soberness'.

a: Valens, who was once made an elder among you
p: An elder of Philippi who fell into greed. All we know of him is in this chapter.
b: Latin qui presbyter factus est aliquando apud vos, 'who was once made an elder among you'. Polycarp says Valens 'understands so little of the place he was given', warns against avaritia, 'greed', and grieves for him 'and for his wife' (11:4). The details of the fault are not given. The 'once' (aliquando) may mean that he no longer held the office, or only that he had been ordained at some earlier time; the letter does not say which. Read with the warnings of 2:2-6:1 against love of money, the case seems to be the trouble behind much of the letter. P. N. Harrison called chapters 1-12 Polycarp's 'Crisis Letter' (1936; so too his reply of 1948).

a: keep away from greed
p: Latin avaritia probably translates Polycarp's philargyria, 'love of money', but the Greek is lost.
b: The Latin translator used avaritia, 'greed, avarice', for whatever Polycarp wrote. In the Greek chapters Polycarp's word for this sin is philargyria, 'love of money' (2:2; 4:1; 4:3; 6:1), and he also uses pleonexia, 'greed' (2:2). Either may lie behind the Latin. The Plain English Translation translates the Latin as it stands, 'greed', and this note marks the link to the earlier warnings.

a: Keep away from every evil
p: 1 Thessalonians 5:22, a letter to Philippi's neighbor church.
b: "Keep away from evil in every form" (1 Thessalonians 5:22). Polycarp's 'keep away' (Latin abstinere, Greek apechesthai in 2:2, 5:3 and 6:1) is the letter's watchword.

a: he will be stained by idolatry
p: Paul's teaching that greed is a form of idol worship (Ephesians 5:5; Colossians 3:5).
b: Paul says: "put to death ... greed, since greed is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5), and in Ephesians 5:5 that no one who is 'greedy (and greed is idolatry)' has an inheritance in the kingdom. Polycarp draws the consequence: the greedy man is defiled by idolatry and will be 'judged as one of the Gentiles', whose worship of idols was the mark of being outside God's people. Jesus said you cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24).

a: who do not know the Lord's judgment
p: The Gentiles 'do not know the Lord's judgment', a phrase from Jeremiah.
b: Jeremiah says of Jerusalem's poor that 'they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God' (Jeremiah 5:4); the Greek Jeremiah has krisin theou, 'the judgment of God', which the Latin iudicium domini matches. Polycarp applies it to the Gentiles in general.

a: the saints will judge the world
p: 1 Corinthians 6:2, introduced with 'as Paul teaches'.
b: "Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" (1 Corinthians 6:2). Polycarp keeps Paul's question form and names his source: 'as Paul teaches' (sicut Paulus docet). If the saints are to judge the world, they must not be judged with the world. Polycarp names Paul as the source here; in 12:1 he speaks of 'these Scriptures'.

a: you who are at the beginning of his letter
t: At the beginning of his letter
p: The Latin is obscure. Lake thinks the Greek meant 'who were his letters in the beginning' (2 Corinthians 3:2).
b: The Latin qui estis in principio epistulae eius most simply means 'you who are (praised) at the beginning of his letter', pointing to Paul's warm thanks in Philippians 1:3-11. Lake's footnote: 'The Greek was perhaps tois ousin en archē epistolais autou, and ought to be rendered "who were his epistles in the beginning", with a reference to II Cor. 3, 2', where Paul tells the Corinthians, "You yourselves are our letter" (2 Corinthians 3:2). Lightfoot's English follows that guess. The Plain English Translation translates the Latin as Lake prints it (variant entry).
orig: qui estis in principio epistulae eius

a: he boasts about you in all the churches
p: The words are those of 2 Thessalonians 1:4, written to Thessalonica, a neighbor of Philippi.
b: Lake's margin gives 2 Thessalonians 1:4: 'we ourselves speak proudly of you among the churches of God'. Paul wrote that to Thessalonica, another Macedonian city, not to Philippi. Polycarp may be remembering it loosely, or thinking of Paul's praise of the Macedonian churches together, such as 2 Corinthians 8:1-2 and 9:2 ('I have been bragging about it to the Macedonians'). Philippians 4:15 says that in the early days only Philippi shared with Paul in giving and receiving.

a: we had not yet come to know him
p: When Paul wrote, the church at Smyrna did not yet exist.
b: Polycarp says the churches Paul boasted of were the only ones that 'knew the Lord at that time', and 'we', the church of Smyrna, 'had not yet come to know him'. Paul worked in Ephesus, not far from Smyrna, for two years, so that 'everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word' (Acts 19:10), but no letter of Paul's names Smyrna. Revelation, written later, addresses the church there (Revelation 2:8-11). Polycarp's words, if taken strictly, put the founding of Smyrna's church after Paul's early letters.

a: May the Lord grant them true repentance
p: 2 Timothy 2:25: God may grant repentance to opponents.
b: Paul tells Timothy to correct opponents gently: "Perhaps God will grant them repentance, so that they come to know the truth" (2 Timothy 2:25). Polycarp prays the same for Valens and his wife, and adds 'true'. The wife's share in the fault is not explained; the prayer includes her.

a: Do not treat such people as enemies
p: 2 Thessalonians 3:15, with Paul's picture of the body.
b: "But do not treat him like an enemy. Correct him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Polycarp's Latin, non sicut inimicos tales existimetis, is plural. Instead he gives a body picture: call them back as members 'who can be hurt and who have wandered' (passibilia membra et errantia), so that the whole body is saved (compare 1 Corinthians 12:26: "When one part hurts, every part hurts along with it"). How a church should treat an unrepentant member is the question of the site's cards at 2 Thessalonians 3, 1 Corinthians 5 and Matthew 18.

a: members who can be hurt
p: Latin passibilia: 'able to suffer'. Lake says 'fallible', Lightfoot 'frail'.
b: Passibilis is 'capable of suffering, liable to feeling'. Polycarp's lost Greek may have had a word for weakness or for suffering. The point is that the fallen are not enemies outside the body but members inside it, hurt and astray, still part of the one body.

a: as it is said in these Scriptures
p: Polycarp quotes Psalm 4 and Ephesians 4:26 together as 'these Scriptures'.
b: Latin ut his scripturis dictum est. 'Be angry, but do not sin' is the Greek Psalm 4 (Hebrew Psalm 4:4, which the site renders from the Hebrew "Be shaken, but do not sin"), and Paul quotes it in Ephesians 4:26; 'Do not let the sun set on your anger' is Paul's own line. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Ephesians 4:26 wording. If 'these Scriptures' covers both lines, Polycarp counts Ephesians as Scripture (compare 2 Peter 3:16, where Paul's letters stand beside 'the other Scriptures'). If he means the Psalm and adds Paul, it does not. The Latin cannot settle which, and the Greek is lost. Topic: canon.

a: you have had good training in the sacred writings
p: Lake thinks Polycarp is quoting the Philippians' own letter back to them.
b: Latin in sacris literis, 'in the sacred letters', the phrase 2 Timothy 3:15 uses of Timothy's Scriptures ('you have known the holy writings'). Lake's footnote: 'Probably this ought to be regarded as a quotation from the letter of the Philippians to Polycarp.' If so, Polycarp is answering a compliment with modesty: he, unlike them, has not been given such learning ('That has not been given to me'), yet he goes on to quote.

a: the eternal high priest himself
p: A title from Hebrews; the Martyrdom of Polycarp uses it in Polycarp's last prayer.
b: Latin sempiternus pontifex, 'everlasting high priest'. Hebrews calls Jesus 'high priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek' (Hebrews 6:20; compare Hebrews 7:3). In the Martyrdom of Polycarp, Polycarp's prayer at the stake praises God 'through the eternal and heavenly high priest Jesus Christ' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 14:3). The Latin word is pontifex, also the title of Rome's own chief priests.
r: Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:3; Hebrews 7:24-26; Martyrdom of Polycarp 14:3

a: our Lord and God Jesus Christ
p: Polycarp calls Jesus 'our Lord and God'; some Latin manuscripts leave out 'and God'.
b: Latin in dominum nostrum et deum Iesum Christum. Lake's footnote: 'Et deum is omitted by some of the MSS of L' (see the variant entry). With 'and God' the phrase matches Thomas's confession, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Titus 2:13. In 6:2 the Greek 'the Lord and God' may also refer to Christ.

a: a share and a portion among his saints
p: Colossians 1:12: the Father has made us fit to share in 'the lot of the saints'.
b: Latin sortem et partem, 'lot and portion', the language of Israel's tribes receiving their land by lot (Numbers 26:55; Deuteronomy 10:9). Colossians 1:12 says the Father 'has made you fit to share in the lot of the saints in the light', and Acts 26:18 speaks of 'an inheritance among those who have been made holy'. Polycarp prays it for the Philippians, for 'us', and for everyone who will yet believe.

a: with patience, long-suffering, endurance
p: Latin patientia, longanimitas, tolerantia. The Greek words behind them are lost.
b: The Latin has three near-synonyms: patientia, 'patience'; longanimitas, 'long-mindedness', slowness to lose patience; and tolerantia, 'bearing up'. Polycarp's Greek is lost here, so which Greek words they stood for cannot be known, and the Plain English Translation renders the Latin words one by one. It does not use 'forbearance', which the site keeps for Greek epieikeia. Lightfoot's English, made from the same Latin, has 'forbearance and long suffering and patient endurance'.
orig: in patientia et in longanimitate et tolerantia

a: Pray also for kings, for authorities and rulers
p: Lake: 'kings' is the regular title of the Roman emperor.
b: 1 Timothy 2:1-2 asks for prayers 'for kings and for all who hold high office'. Lake's footnote: 'Pro regibus is no doubt a translation of hyper basileōn and basileus is regularly used as the title of the Emperor.' Polycarp asks the Philippians to pray for the emperors whose governors could send Christians to death, and in the same breath for 'those who persecute you and hate you' (12:3), as Jesus told his disciples to 'pray for the people who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44). The Martyrdom shows him at his trial saying Christians give rulers the honor that is due (Martyrdom of Polycarp 10:2).
r: 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Matthew 5:44; Martyrdom of Polycarp 10:2

a: for those who persecute you and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross
p: Jesus' command to pray for persecutors, and Paul's 'enemies of Christ's cross'.
b: "keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44); Luke 6:27 adds 'the people who hate you'. 'The enemies of the cross' is Paul's phrase to this same church: 'they are the enemies of Christ's cross' (Philippians 3:18). Paul wept over them; Polycarp asks for prayer for them.

a: You wrote to me, both you and Ignatius
p: Ignatius asked the churches to send messengers and letters to Antioch, whose church was now at peace.
b: Here the Greek returns, from Eusebius (Church History 3.36.14-15). Ignatius had written to Polycarp that 'the Church which is at Antioch in Syria is ... at peace', and asked him to choose a messenger 'that he may go into Syria' and to write to the nearby churches 'that they also may act in like manner, such as are able to do so sending messengers, and the others transmitting letters through those persons who are sent by you' (To Polycarp 7-8, ANF translation). The Philippians, it seems, got the same request and asked Polycarp to carry their letter.

a: someone I send as an envoy
p: Greek presbeuonta: one who goes as an ambassador.
b: The verb presbeuō, 'act as an envoy', is Paul's in 2 Corinthians 5:20 ('we are ambassadors for Christ'). Ignatius had called the messenger to Syria 'God's runner' (Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2, Greek theodromos; the ANF has 'the messenger of God'). The future participle shows Polycarp still planning the trip when he wrote, a detail that matters for the date of this chapter (see the chapter page).

a: They are attached to this letter
p: Polycarp sent the Philippians copies of Ignatius's letters with this one; Lake says the Philippians wanted to make a collection of them.
b: Lake says the letter 'appears to have been immediately called for by the desire of the Philippians to make a collection of the letters of Ignatius', and calls it 'as we should say, a "covering letter"' for the copies he sent 'of all the Ignatian epistles to which he had access'. Eusebius lists seven letters of Ignatius: to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians and Romans, written from Smyrna, and to the Philadelphians, the Smyrnaeans and Polycarp, written from Troas (Church History 3.36.5-10). Lake adds that the one letter Polycarp and the Philippians could not easily have obtained would be the one to the Romans, and that this letter 'seems to have had a different textual history from that of the other six'.

a: let us know anything more certain you have learned about Ignatius himself
p: This line, in Latin only, seems to speak of Ignatius as alive; 9:2 counts him among the dead.
b: The Latin de his qui cum eo sunt, 'those who are with him', sounds as if Ignatius is still on his way. Two answers: (1) one letter: Polycarp knew Ignatius was condemned and wrote of him in 9:2 as one whose death was certain, while asking here for firm news (the Catholic Encyclopedia's view: written 'before he had heard of St. Ignatius' martyrdom'); (2) two letters: P. N. Harrison (1936) took chapter 13 as an early 'Covering Note' and 1-12 as a 'Crisis Letter' about 135-137; C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd accepted two letters but put the second only months or a year or two later (Harrison's reply, 1948). To Dodd's question, 'Are not Ignatius's companions still "with him" in heaven?', Harrison answered that the phrase reads so only by 'tearing it out of its context' in the Covering Note (1948).

a: by the hand of Crescens
p: A man of Smyrna who carried the letter to Philippi, with his sister.
b: Latin per Crescentem, 'through Crescens'. Letters were carried by trusted travelers, who were commended in the letter itself, as Paul commended Phoebe (Romans 16:1: 'Let me recommend to you Phoebe, our sister'). A Crescens appears in 2 Timothy 4:10 ('Crescens went to Galatia'); the name was common, and nothing in either text links the two. Polycarp also commends Crescens's sister, who would travel later; women moved between churches and needed the same welcome.

a: I commended him to you a little while ago
p: Latin in praesenti: 'just now', or 'when I was with you'?
b: The Latin quem in praesenti commendavi vobis et nunc commendo is unclear. In praesenti often means 'at present, for now', which here suggests a recent commendation. Lake renders 'whom I commended to you when I was present', as if Polycarp had been in Philippi, which the letter nowhere else suggests. Lightfoot renders 'recently'. The Plain English Translation follows the sense 'a little while ago'.
